title: Step 12: Search across requirements (full-text + trigram)
summary: One search box, three matchers: a code prefix, Turkish words (stems or prefixes, lowered with Turkish rules on both sides) and a folded trigram key for typos and English keyboards. Results come in tiers, ranked, paged by a keyset cursor.

examples.title: Migration 005, and which matcher finds what people actually type

annotations.note: Both are trusted extensions: a role with CREATE privilege on the database, such as its owner, may create them without being a superuser (step 15 sets up that role). IF NOT EXISTS because another application may already have installed them in this database.

lower() follows the database's locale; TraceLite's runs on whatever the customer's server has, which, unless it is a Turkish locale, maps I to i. Naming the ICU Turkish collation makes the result the same everywhere: I to ı, İ to i. The function is the one place where that rule lives.
sql.search.trigram's folded key: ı, i, I and İ all become i, ş becomes s. It is the answer to users who type IKI ADIMLI or sifre, and it is used only for matching, never for display.

The query side. plainto_tsquery ANDs the stems of the typed words; the second half ANDs every word as a prefix (:*). || between two tsqueries is OR. The words are cut at anything that isn't a letter or a digit, and quote_literal makes each one a single lexeme, so no input can be read as tsquery syntax.

One stored vector, two spellings of every word: the Turkish stem and the word itself. The stemmer catches inflections (girişte is giriş); the words catch what it cuts too far (parola becomes parol) and make prefixes work. The title weighs A, the description B, for ranking.

One GIN index per matcher: the tsvector for words, a trigram index on the folded title for typos. Codes need no new index: the B-tree of requirements_code_key already serves prefix ranges (example 3).

tr_lower turned KARANLIK into karanlık before the stemmer saw it; lower() would have made it karanlik, a word nobody types. Stems and words differ in the description (kullan, kullanımı), and the stemmer errs on short words: gece (night) became geç (late), koyu (dark) became ko. The whole word is still there to match.

A user with caps lock on a Turkish keyboard types SIFIRLAMA with dotless I, and tr_lower gives sıfırla, the same lexeme as in the column. A user who has typed only paro gets a prefix query that already finds parola.

A code prefix is a range on codes: COLLATE "C" upper-cases only ASCII, as codes need (step 2's pitfall), and every code that starts with AUTH-L lies between AUTH-L and AUTH-L~, because the code CHECK allows only characters that sort before ~. An empty input would match every code, so the API refuses q="".

Each matcher finds what the others can't: auth-l only as a code; parolalar through its stem (parola, matching the word parola); paro and e-posta as prefixes; IKI ADIMLI and the typo sifirlma only through the folded trigram key. Trigrams look at titles only, which is why e-posta (in descriptions) isn't found that way.
The bug tr_lower prevents: lowered with the database's rules, SIFIRLAMA becomes sifirla, which is not in any vector, and caps-lock users find nothing.

examples.title: One query, three tiers, ranked, and paged by a keyset over the ranking

annotations.note: queries/search.sql, prepared exactly as pgx prepares it. Each row matched by any matcher gets a tier (1 code, 2 words, 3 similar) and an integer score; the order is tier, score descending, then code, which is unique per project and makes the order total.
Scores are ts_rank or word_similarity scaled to integers. Floats in a cursor would have to survive JSON and a round trip to compare equal; integers do. Code hits all score 0 and come in code order.

The typed text is turned into a prefix, a tsquery and a key once, in a one-row subquery, so each matcher's condition below is written once and compares a column with a value fixed for the whole query.
The keyset, as in step 4: a row comparison with the last row's key. Negating the score turns its descending order into ascending, so one row comparison expresses tier ASC, score DESC, code ASC.
A code hit comes first, then title hits by rank. AUTH-LOGIN outranks AUTH-RESET because its description mentions parolasıyla as well; the fourth row only says that a next page exists.

Page 2 continues from the cursor. Three rows tie on score, since each mentions the word once in its description; the code breaks the tie, the same way on every request. Three rows are fewer than four: this is the last page.
A typo plus an English keyboard: no code, no word matches, and the folded trigram key still finds the title, in tier 3.

examples.title: Which index serves which matcher, in the generic plans pgx ends up with

annotations.note: The range is the code matcher's form because it uses the B-tree with $2 unknown: both bounds are expressions of a parameter, which an index condition accepts.

The same matcher as LIKE: with a literal pattern the planner derives the same range itself, but here the pattern is only known at run time, so it reads every row of the project and filters. psql shows the good plan; the application, after five executions, may get this one.
tr_lower has been inlined, which keeps the expression usable in an index condition; EXPLAIN doesn't print its COLLATE. The GIN index answers @@ for any query value.
<% (word_similarity above pg_trgm.word_similarity_threshold, 0.6 by default) is served by the trigram GIN index through its commutator %>, with the exact score checked on the rows it returns.

Ordering by trigram distance is a different job: GIN can only filter, so this sorts the whole table. A GiST trigram index can return rows in distance order; TraceLite doesn't need it, since its similar tier is filtered first and sorted afterwards.

use_cases: A search box over records with short identifiers and prose fields: tickets, products, documents, requirements
Turkish or mixed-keyboard users: caps lock with dotless I, phones without Turkish letters, copy-pasted text
Type-ahead: prefixes of every word and of codes, answered from indexes on each keystroke after a short debounce
Search results in a paged API whose pages must stay stable while other users edit
strengths: No search engine to run or keep in sync: the vector is a generated column, updated in the same transaction as the row
Each failure mode of typing has its own matcher, and the tier says which one fired, so the UI can show 'did you mean' for tier 3
Turkish lowering lives in one SQL function used by the column and every query, so the two sides can't drift
Integer scores and a code tiebreaker give a total order that keyset pagination can use unchanged from step 4
weaknesses: Every page ranks all matches again; keyset pagination keeps pages stable, not cheap
ts_rank has no notion of rare words (no IDF), so a requirement that repeats a common word can outrank a better one
Two spellings per word make the vector and its GIN index roughly twice as large
The folded key merges distinct Turkish words (kır and kir), so tier 3 can return surprises; it is a fallback, ranked last

pitfalls.title: LIKE with a parameter for prefix search
pitfalls.detail: code LIKE $1 || '%' uses the B-tree only when the planner sees a constant pattern. pgx prepares statements, and after five executions PostgreSQL may switch to a generic plan that scans the whole project. Write the prefix as a range, which an index condition accepts with parameters.
pitfalls.good: WHERE project_id = $1 AND code >= $2 AND code < $2 || '~'  -- codes contain only characters below ~

pitfalls.title: Lowering the document and the query differently
pitfalls.detail: If the column uses tr_lower and the query plain lower() (or Go's strings.ToLower), IŞIK becomes ışık in the column and işik in the query, and nothing matches. One SQL function, called on both sides.

pitfalls.title: Building tsquery text from user input
pitfalls.detail: to_tsquery('simple', $1 || ':*') fails with a syntax error on input like 'parola & (' and lets users write operators. Split the input into words in SQL, quote each with quote_literal, and append :* to each.

pitfalls.title: Floats in a keyset cursor
pitfalls.detail: A ts_rank of 0.6079271 that went through JSON and came back as a parameter may not compare equal to the value recomputed by the query, and the page boundary repeats or skips a row. Scale scores to integers before they become part of the sort key.

pitfalls.title: Searching on unaccent alone
pitfalls.detail: The folded key finds sifre for şifre, but also merges kır and kir and defeats the Turkish stemmer. Keep it as the last tier, after code and word matches.

quiz.q: A user with caps lock on types PAROLA SIFIRLAMA. Why does the word matcher find Parola sıfırlama only with tr_lower?
options: lower() maps I to i, giving sifirla, while the column holds sıfırla
quiz.why: The database's lowering isn't Turkish; tr_lower maps I to ı on both sides, so the lexemes agree.

quiz.q: Why does the code matcher use code >= $2 AND code < $2 || '~' instead of LIKE $2 || '%'?
options: With a parameter, the planner can't turn LIKE into an index range, and pgx's prepared statements may get a generic plan
quiz.why: B-tree prefix matching for LIKE requires a constant pattern at planning time; a range with parameters is an index condition in any plan.

quiz.q: Which matcher finds IKI ADIMLI typed on an English keyboard?
quiz.why: tr_lower makes it ıkı adımlı, which isn't iki adımlı; folding both sides with unaccent gives iki adimli, which the trigram index matches.

quiz.q: Why are scores scaled to integers before they go into the cursor?
options: So the cursor's value compares equal to the recomputed score, and pages neither repeat nor skip rows
quiz.why: The keyset condition compares the cursor with values the query computes again; integers survive the round trip exactly.

body:
## Concept

People don't search like a `WHERE` clause. They type half a code (`auth-l`), a word in
a different form than the title uses (`parolalar`), the start of a word (`paro`), a
title with caps lock on a Turkish keyboard (`PAROLA SIFIRLAMA`), or with no Turkish
letters at all, and with typos (`sifirlma`). TraceLite's search runs three matchers
over a project's requirements and merges them into one ranked list:

1. **Code prefix** (tier 1): `upper(q)` as a range over `code`, served by the existing
   `requirements_code_key` B-tree.
2. **Words** (tier 2): a stored `tsvector` holding, for title (weight A) and description
   (B), both the Turkish stem and the whole word of every word. The query asks for all
   typed words as stems, or all of them as prefixes. Both sides are lowered with
   Turkish rules by one function, `tr_lower`. Ranked with `ts_rank`.
3. **Similar** (tier 3): `word_similarity` between folded keys (`search_key`, which maps
   ş to s and ı, I, İ to i) of the input and the title, through a trigram index. Ranked
   by the similarity.

A row matched by several matchers counts in its best tier. Within a tier, a higher
score comes first; the code breaks ties. That sort key is also the cursor.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Elasticsearch/Lucene**: the three tiers are a `bool` query with `should` clauses
  (a `prefix` on a keyword field, a `match` on a Turkish-analyzed field, a `fuzzy`
  match), and the tiers stand in for boosts. Lucene scores with BM25 and has a Turkish
  lowercase filter; PostgreSQL's `ts_rank` has no IDF, and Turkish lowering is
  `tr_lower`. In exchange there is no index refresh and nothing to keep in sync.
- **Java/Hibernate Search, Python/django-watson**: both keep a search index next to the
  ORM. Here the index is a generated column, so a raw SQL update or the step 7 importer
  updates it too.
- **JS (Fuse.js, match-sorter)**: fuzzy search in the browser over data already
  loaded. Fine for a hundred rows; TraceLite searches on the server so that the page
  never needs all requirements.
- **Go**: `strings.ToLower` uses Unicode's default mapping (I to i), like the database's
  `lower()`; `golang.org/x/text/cases.Lower(language.Turkish)` is `tr_lower`'s
  equivalent. TraceLite lowers only in SQL, so Go never sees the question.

## How it works

`migrations/005_search.sql` is example 1's middle part. The endpoint, in `openapi.yaml`:

```yaml
  /api/projects/{projectId}/requirement-search:
    parameters: [{ $ref: "#/components/parameters/ProjectId" }]
    get:
      operationId: searchRequirements
      parameters:
        - { name: q, in: query, required: true, schema: { type: string, minLength: 1, maxLength: 100 } }
        - { $ref: "#/components/parameters/Limit" }
        - { $ref: "#/components/parameters/Cursor" }
      responses:
        "200":
          description: Best matches first
          content: { application/json: { schema: { $ref: "#/components/schemas/SearchPage" } } }
        "400": { $ref: "#/components/responses/Problem" }   # q blank or too long, bad cursor
        "404": { $ref: "#/components/responses/Problem" }
# components.schemas:
    SearchHit:
      allOf:
        - { $ref: "#/components/schemas/Requirement" }
        - type: object
          required: [match]
          properties: { match: { type: string, enum: [code, words, similar] } }
    SearchPage:
      type: object
      required: [items, nextCursor]
      properties:
        items: { type: array, items: { $ref: "#/components/schemas/SearchHit" } }
        nextCursor: { type: [string, "null"] }
```

The handler trims `q` and refuses it when blank (400; an empty prefix would match every
code), decodes the cursor into `[tier, score, code]` (step 4's format: base64url JSON,
the last row's sort key), runs `SearchRequirements` with `limit+1` and maps the tier to
`match`. The request path is the same as the list's; only the query differs.

Which index serves which matcher (example 3):

| Matcher | Condition | Index |
|---|---|---|
| code | `code >= $p AND code < $p \|\| '~'` | `requirements_code_key` (B-tree, from step 2) |
| words | `search @@ words_query($q)` | `requirements_search` (GIN on the tsvector) |
| similar | `search_key($q) <% search_key(title)` | `requirements_title_key` (GIN, `gin_trgm_ops`) |

For a project of a few hundred requirements the planner may well read the project's
rows through `requirements_code_key` and check all three conditions on each, which can
cost less than three index scans; the plan depends on the statistics. The GIN indexes start to matter in big projects, and they
are what make a search across all projects possible later.

In the browser, the search box waits 200 ms after the last keystroke, then runs a
`useInfiniteQuery` keyed `["projects", projectId, "search", q]` with
`placeholderData: keepPreviousData`, so the old results stay on screen while the new
ones load. The key sits under the project prefix, so step 9's events refresh open
results too. Each hit shows its `match` as a small label: `kod`, `kelime`, `benzer`.

## Design notes

**Three matchers, not one clever one.** A single trigram search over code, title and
description would find most things, ranked by an opaque similarity. Separate matchers
make each rule explainable ("codes match by prefix", "words match by stem or start",
"everything else by similarity") and let the UI say why a result is there. The order of
the tiers encodes what users mean: a typed code is a precise request; a fuzzy match is a
guess.

**Turkish rules in one function.** `tr_lower` names the ICU Turkish collation, so the
behavior doesn't depend on how the customer's PostgreSQL was initialized. The same
function lowers the stored vector and every query; Go code never lowers search text.
`search_key` deliberately does the opposite (it forgets Turkish letters) and is used
only where that is the point.

**Keyset over a ranking.** The cursor holds the last row's (tier, score, code). That
keeps pages stable when requirements are added between requests, and it is the same
cursor format as every other list. It doesn't make later pages cheaper: each page
ranks all matches again. A search returns tens of rows, not thousands, so that cost is
accepted; past that, a smaller `limit` on deep pages or a cap on matches would come
first.

**Not done here.** Highlighting the matched words is `ts_headline` (sql.search.fts),
called for the page's rows only. A "did you mean" for queries with no results would
offer the nearest word from `ts_stat` over the project's vectors, as the pg_trgm docs
suggest. Synonyms (şifre for parola) need a synonym dictionary file on the server, which
a migration can't install.

files.examples/01_search_columns.sql:
-- LEARN(fullstack.tracelite.step-12-search): Turkish lowering on both sides, stems plus words in one tsvector, a folded trigram key for other keyboards.
CREATE TABLE requirements (  -- step 2's table, abridged
  project_id  int NOT NULL,
  code        text COLLATE "C" NOT NULL,
  title       text NOT NULL,
  description text NOT NULL DEFAULT '',
  CONSTRAINT requirements_code_key UNIQUE (project_id, code)
);

-- migrations/005_search.sql
-- +goose Up
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pg_trgm;
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS unaccent;
CREATE FUNCTION tr_lower(text) RETURNS text  -- I to ı, İ to i, whatever the database's locale
  LANGUAGE sql IMMUTABLE PARALLEL SAFE STRICT
  RETURN lower($1 COLLATE "tr-x-icu");
CREATE FUNCTION search_key(text) RETURNS text  -- for keyboards without Turkish letters
  LANGUAGE sql IMMUTABLE PARALLEL SAFE STRICT
  RETURN lower(unaccent('unaccent'::regdictionary, $1));
CREATE FUNCTION words_query(q text) RETURNS tsquery  -- every word as a stem, or every word as a prefix
  LANGUAGE sql STABLE PARALLEL SAFE STRICT
  RETURN plainto_tsquery('turkish', tr_lower(q)) ||
    (SELECT to_tsquery('simple', string_agg(quote_literal(w) || ':*', ' & '))
     FROM regexp_split_to_table(tr_lower(q), '[^[:alnum:]]+') AS w WHERE w <> '');
ALTER TABLE requirements ADD COLUMN search tsvector GENERATED ALWAYS AS (
  setweight(to_tsvector('turkish', tr_lower(title)) || to_tsvector('simple', tr_lower(title)), 'A') ||
  setweight(to_tsvector('turkish', tr_lower(description)) || to_tsvector('simple', tr_lower(description)), 'B')
) STORED;
CREATE INDEX requirements_search ON requirements USING gin (search);
CREATE INDEX requirements_title_key ON requirements USING gin (search_key(title) gin_trgm_ops);
-- end of 005_search.sql

INSERT INTO requirements (project_id, code, title, description) VALUES
  (1, 'AUTH',               'Kimlik doğrulama', ''),
  (1, 'AUTH-LOGIN',         'Parola ile giriş', 'Kullanıcı e-posta adresi ve parolasıyla giriş yapar.'),
  (1, 'AUTH-LOGIN-2FA',     'İki adımlı doğrulama', 'Girişte SMS ile tek kullanımlık kod istenir.'),
  (1, 'AUTH-LOGIN-LOCKOUT', 'Hatalı girişte hesap kilitleme', 'Beş hatalı denemeden sonra hesap kilitlenir.'),
  (1, 'AUTH-RESET',         'Parola sıfırlama', 'Sıfırlama bağlantısı e-postayla gönderilir.'),
  (1, 'UI-DARK',            'KARANLIK TEMA', 'Gece kullanımı için koyu renkler.');

-- What the index holds: stems (turkish) and whole words (simple), title A, description B.
SELECT title, description, search FROM requirements WHERE code = 'UI-DARK';

-- The query side goes through the same tr_lower.
SELECT words_query('Parola sıfırlama') AS turkish_keyboard,
       words_query('PAROLA SIFIRLAMA') AS caps_lock,
       words_query('paro') AS typing;

-- How users type, and which of the three matchers finds what.
SELECT typed,
  (SELECT string_agg(code, ' ' ORDER BY code) FROM requirements
    WHERE code >= upper(typed COLLATE "C") AND code < upper(typed COLLATE "C") || '~') AS by_code,
  (SELECT string_agg(code, ' ' ORDER BY code) FROM requirements
    WHERE search @@ words_query(typed)) AS by_words,
  (SELECT string_agg(code, ' ' ORDER BY code) FROM requirements
    WHERE search_key(typed) <% search_key(title)) AS by_trigram
FROM (VALUES ('auth-l'), ('PAROLA SIFIRLAMA'), ('parolalar'), ('paro'), ('karanlık'),
             ('IKI ADIMLI'), ('sifirlma'), ('kilitlenir'), ('e-posta')) AS t(typed);

-- The caps-lock query again, lowered with the database's rules instead: I becomes i.
SELECT plainto_tsquery('turkish', lower('PAROLA SIFIRLAMA')) AS db_lower,
       plainto_tsquery('turkish', tr_lower('PAROLA SIFIRLAMA')) AS tr_lower;
files.examples/02_ranked_pages.sql:
-- Example 1's table, migration 005 and words_query, condensed.
CREATE EXTENSION pg_trgm;
CREATE EXTENSION unaccent;
CREATE FUNCTION tr_lower(text) RETURNS text LANGUAGE sql IMMUTABLE PARALLEL SAFE STRICT
  RETURN lower($1 COLLATE "tr-x-icu");
CREATE FUNCTION search_key(text) RETURNS text LANGUAGE sql IMMUTABLE PARALLEL SAFE STRICT
  RETURN lower(unaccent('unaccent'::regdictionary, $1));
CREATE FUNCTION words_query(q text) RETURNS tsquery LANGUAGE sql STABLE PARALLEL SAFE STRICT
  RETURN plainto_tsquery('turkish', tr_lower(q)) ||
    (SELECT to_tsquery('simple', string_agg(quote_literal(w) || ':*', ' & '))
     FROM regexp_split_to_table(tr_lower(q), '[^[:alnum:]]+') AS w WHERE w <> '');
CREATE TABLE requirements (
  project_id int NOT NULL, code text COLLATE "C" NOT NULL, title text NOT NULL,
  description text NOT NULL DEFAULT '',
  search tsvector GENERATED ALWAYS AS (
    setweight(to_tsvector('turkish', tr_lower(title)) || to_tsvector('simple', tr_lower(title)), 'A') ||
    setweight(to_tsvector('turkish', tr_lower(description)) || to_tsvector('simple', tr_lower(description)), 'B')
  ) STORED,
  CONSTRAINT requirements_code_key UNIQUE (project_id, code));
CREATE INDEX requirements_search ON requirements USING gin (search);
CREATE INDEX requirements_title_key ON requirements USING gin (search_key(title) gin_trgm_ops);

INSERT INTO requirements (project_id, code, title, description) VALUES
  (1, 'AUTH-LOGIN',         'Parola ile giriş', 'Kullanıcı e-posta adresi ve parolasıyla giriş yapar.'),
  (1, 'AUTH-LOGIN-LOCKOUT', 'Hatalı girişte hesap kilitleme', 'Beş hatalı parola denemesinden sonra hesap kilitlenir.'),
  (1, 'AUTH-RESET',         'Parola sıfırlama', 'Sıfırlama bağlantısı e-postayla gönderilir.'),
  (1, 'AUTH-RESET-EXPIRY',  'Sıfırlama bağlantısının süresi', 'Bağlantı bir saat sonra geçersizdir; yeni parola istenir.'),
  (1, 'PAROLA-KURAL',       'Parola kuralları', 'En az on iki karakter.'),
  (1, 'PROFILE',            'Profil sayfası', 'Kullanıcı adını ve parolasını değiştirebilir.');

-- queries/search.sql, SearchRequirements. $1 project, $2 what the user typed,
-- $3-$5 the last row's sort key (tier 0 on the first page), $6 page size + 1.
PREPARE search(int, text, int, int, text, int) AS
SELECT tier, score, code, title
FROM (
  SELECT r.code, r.title,
    CASE WHEN r.code >= q.prefix AND r.code < q.prefix || '~' THEN 1
         WHEN r.search @@ q.words THEN 2
         ELSE 3 END AS tier,
    CASE WHEN r.code >= q.prefix AND r.code < q.prefix || '~' THEN 0
         WHEN r.search @@ q.words THEN (1e6 * ts_rank(r.search, q.words))::int
         ELSE (1e6 * word_similarity(q.key, search_key(r.title)))::int END AS score
  FROM (SELECT upper($2 COLLATE "C") AS prefix, words_query($2) AS words, search_key($2) AS key) AS q,
       requirements AS r
  WHERE r.project_id = $1
    AND (r.code >= q.prefix AND r.code < q.prefix || '~'
         OR r.search @@ q.words
         OR q.key <% search_key(r.title))
) AS hits
WHERE (tier, -score, code) > ($3, -$4, $5)
ORDER BY tier, score DESC, code
LIMIT $6;

-- Page 1 of "parola", three per page: the API asks for four.
EXECUTE search(1, 'parola', 0, 0, '', 4);
-- Page 2: after the third row's key, which nextCursor carried as [2, 607927, "AUTH-RESET"].
EXECUTE search(1, 'parola', 2, 607927, 'AUTH-RESET', 4);
-- Typed with a typo, and typed on an English keyboard.
EXECUTE search(1, 'sifirlma baglantisi', 0, 0, '', 4);
